# nb — read Jupyter notebooks without context bloat

Use `nb` instead of Read/cat on any `.ipynb`. A measurement notebook carries
megabytes of base64 plot output; reading the raw JSON burns the context window on
data you cannot see anyway. `nb` shows structure and source, and renders outputs
as size-annotated placeholders.

Installed on PATH by `install.sh`. Stdlib-only, so it also runs directly as
`~/sharpelab/sharpelab-shared/tools/nb.py`.

## Usage

Cell indices are 0-based and match `nb['cells'][i]` in the raw JSON. Ranges accept
`30-80`, `5,12,30-`, or a bare index.

```bash
nb sections <file.ipynb>          # markdown-header outline with cell indices
nb summary  <file.ipynb> [range]  # per-cell table: type, exec count, size, preview
nb stats    <file.ipynb>          # totals and the heaviest cells
nb cells    <file.ipynb> <range>  # full source of those cells
nb cells    <file.ipynb> <range> --outputs   # include outputs and error tracebacks
nb grep     <file.ipynb> <regex>  # search cell source; --type code|md, -i
nb extract  <file.ipynb> <range>  # write embedded images out; --out DIR, --mime MIME
```

## Approach

Work top-down — it is normal to answer a question without ever reading a cell in
full:

1. `nb sections` to see the notebook's shape, or `nb grep` to jump straight to the
   cells that mention what you care about.
2. `nb summary` over the region of interest to see which cells actually ran
   (execution count) and which carry heavy output.
3. `nb cells <range>` for the source that matters.

Add `--outputs` only once you know the cell is small, or when you specifically
need a result or a traceback — that is the flag that pulls real weight into
context. To look at a figure, `nb extract` it to a file and read the image.
